chunks.content: Introduction The prevalence of individuals living globally with congenital heart disease has increased by 18.7% from 1990 to 2017, which is related to improved outcomes and population growth [ ]. Correspondingly, in China, the scale of pediatric cardiac care is substantial. According to the “2023 White Book of Chinese Cardiovascular Surgery and Extracorporeal Circulation,” a total of 43,909 cardiovascular surgeries were performed on patients under the age of 18 in 2023 [ ]. This volume underscores an acute and growing need for standardized training protocols for clinical practitioners. Transesophageal Echocardiography (TEE) is indispensable in this field, playing a key role in the intraoperative guidance and evaluation of cardiac surgeries, which has been shown to significantly reduce mortality and morbidity [ ]. Consequently, it is imperative for pediatric cardiac anesthesiologists to achieve high competency in TEE techniques and the accurate interpretation of images during the perioperative period [ ]. Traditionally, TEE training occurs within the operating room (OR) through an apprenticeship model. However, the OR is a high-stress environment that inherently introduces risks when novice trainees perform TEE maneuvers—a concern particularly acute in pediatric patients due to their fragile anatomical structures. These risks include mechanical trauma, such as esophageal mucosal injury or life-threatening perforation, and airway complications like subglottic edema or vocal cord trauma, which can result in extubation failure [ ]. Additionally, the lack of proficiency in inexperienced operators poses a significant risk of delayed or inaccurate diagnosis, which can negatively impact perioperative management [ ]. To address these challenges, simulation-based medical education has emerged as a promising alternative. This education allows trainees to acquire cognitive and technical procedural skills in a controlled, risk-free environment, potentially improving patient safety and proving more effective than traditional apprenticeship training [ , ]. While the benefits of simulation are recognized, there is limited evidence directly comparing its translation to real-world clinical performance in the demanding field of pediatric TEE. Therefore, the aim of this study was to compare the efficacy of simulation-based training using a dedicated pediatric TEE simulator versus traditional apprenticeship training on live patients, specifically focusing on the improvement of pediatric TEE skills in a real-world clinical setting. Methods Study setting and ethics The study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki (2013 revision). This prospective randomized controlled single-center study was first approved by the Ethics committee of the Institutional Review Board of Guangzhou Women and Children’s Medical Center (GWCMC)([2022]273A2025021300) on Oct30, 2022, however, due to the severe Covid situation and epidemic prevention policies, the project didn’t make any progress. On February 13, 2025, we applied for an extension, and it was approved. The progress then registered at the Chinese Clinical Trial Registry ( www.chictr.org.cn ; ChiCTR2500105325; principal investigator: Yingyi Xu) on July 02, 2025, and conducted from July 03, 2025 to August 07, 2025, in GWCMC, Guangzhou, China. Deidentified data from this study are available from the authors upon request. All trial participants were briefed in advance and signed informed consent. Participants and randomization A convenience sample of 44 first- through third-year anesthesia residents were recruited who had no prior formal training or clinical rotation experience in pediatric transesophageal echocardiography (TEE). Since it was an exploratory clinical study, we did not perform sample size estimates. Participants were randomly assigned (1:1 ratio) to either the Simulation group (Group S, n = 22) or the Traditional group (Group T, n = 22) using a computer-generated randomization sequence (Stata 16.0; Stata Corp, College Station, TX, USA). To minimize bias, outcome assessors and data analysts were blinded to the group allocation and tested-instructors, although trainees and train-instructors could not be blinded due to the nature of the educational intervention. Deidentified data from this study are available upon request. Phase 1: standardized foundational education (Both Groups) Before group allocation–specific training, all participants received identical foundational instruction to ensure comparable baseline knowledge. This phase consisted of: (1) A 2-hour synchronized online didactic session, mandatory for all residents, covering: basic cardiac anatomy and ultrasound physics, principles of pediatric TEE probe handling and the 11 standardized basic perioperative TEE views (Supplementary File 1). There have been previous studies that have successfully used this tool and have also effectively evaluated TEE teaching methods [ ]. Attendance was monitored, and all participants completed at least 2 h of standardized foundational training. Additional voluntary self-study outside these sessions was not tracked and was not considered in the analysis. Phase 2: group-specific hands-on training After completion of the foundational phase, residents were randomized into one of two training pathways. Simulation group (Group S) Residents in Group S received one-on-one simulation-based training using a mannequin-based pediatric TEE simulator (BabyWorks ® , CAE Healthcare). The simulator simultaneously displayed: real-time ultrasound images, probe position and imaging plane orientation and a corresponding three-dimensional cardiac model. This multimodal feedback allowed trainees to directly visualize the relationship between probe manipulation and image acquisition. Training was conducted in a structured sequence: observation of the instructor performing a standardized pediatric TEE examination on the simulator and hands-on practice by the trainee on the simulator under direct supervision, focusing on probe manipulation and acquisition of the 11 basic views. Each training session lasted 1 h per trainee. Traditional group (Group T) Residents in Group T received one-on-one apprenticeship-based training in the operating room during routine pediatric cardiac surgery. Training followed a parallel structure: observation of the instructor performing TEE on a live patient, and hands-on TEE performance by the trainee on patients under direct supervision. Each training session also lasted 1 h per trainee. Phase 3: final live clinical assessment One week after completion of the training phase, all residents from both groups underwent a standardized clinical assessment. Trainees were required to obtain the 11 basic TEE views on live pediatric patients (aged 10–18 months). A maximum time limit of 15 min was imposed. During assessment, instructors provided passive supervision only, intervening solely if probe manipulation posed a safety risk. To ensure objectivity, performance was independently evaluated by two TEE board–certified instructors who had not participated in the prior training sessions and assessments included image quality, anatomical visualization, and acquisition efficiency according to predefined criteria. Performance was evaluated using a structured scoring system adapted from Ferrero et al. Each view was scored on a scale of 0 to 10 based on three dimensions: imaging angle (0–2 points), overall clarity (0–2 points), and visualization of specific anatomical structures (0–6 points), yielding a maximum total score of 110 points (Supplementary File 2) [ ]. All live clinical training and assessment procedures were conducted under the passive supervision of the instructor. The supervisor immediately intervened if any of the following occurred: (1) unsafe probe handling or potential risk to the patient, (2) difficulty advancing or positioning the probe, or (3) urgent clinical or surgical requirements. Given the educational nature of the intervention, no formal adverse event schedule was prespecified. Patient-related procedural complications were monitored according to institutional routine. Data collection After basic Pediatric TEE education, each participant took a multiple-choice test. After completing each stage of the training course, all participants completed a practical exam, which was conducted in the operating room or on the pediatric TEE simulator. The participants received final testing on patients in need of surgery one week after the course. These patients all needed TEE for their surgeries. Each resident needed to present 11 basic images within 15 min, an assessment tool used by Ferrero et. in their previous investigations was used for the evaluations in this study [ , ]. This assessment tool contains 11 basic TEE views. Each view has a defined criterion that ranges from 0 to 2 points, including: imaging angle, overall clarity, and visualization of the 3 major anatomical structures associated with each view. All scores were marked by 2 experienced TEE instructors (board-certified attending anesthesiologists). Scorers and data analysts were unaware of treatment assignment groups, and trainees and train-instructors could not be blinded due to the nature of the educational intervention. The scoring criteria are shown in Supplementary File 3. Statistical analysis A formal a priori sample size calculation was not performed due to the fixed cohort size in the residency program; a convenience sample of 44 trainees was enrolled. This study utilized statistical methods such as Chi-square tests, t-tests, and correlation analysis to evaluate differences between two groups. Categorical variables were compared using the Chi-square test, while continuous variables (e.g., years since graduation and overall scores) were compared using the t-test. Results Participant characteristics A total of 46 residents were screened from July 03 to August 07, 2025. Two residents were excluded owing to unwillingness to continue the training. A total of 44 residents received training. The participants characteristics were comparable across different rate groups (Table ) with no statistically significant differences. We administered the same test on knowledge of esophageal ultrasound to each participant prior to training, and the total scores were similar and not significantly different between the two groups (Table ). TEE operation after training One week after training, we recorded all participants’ TEE performances on pediatric patients who were 10–18 months old and planned to receive percutaneous balloon aortic valvuloplasty. All patients were involved in this trial under their parents’ agreements. No adverse events or patient-related procedural complications were observed in either group during the study period. Group S (mean 88.60) scored significantly higher than Group T (mean 64.70) ( p < 0.001). Furthermore, the examination duration (time required to complete the 11-view protocol) was significantly shorter in Group S (447.60 ± 136.90 s) than in Group T (584.50 ± 180.00 s, p = 0.007) (Table ; Fig. ). The scores of Angle/clarity/structures were compared between the two groups The median of the total Angle score of the 11 landmarks was 19.30 in the Group S and 17.00 in the Group T, and the p -value was 0.031. In the total clarity score of 11 landmarks, the median score of Group S was 17.30, and that of Group T was 11.90 ( p < 0.001). Similarly, in the structural score, the median total score was 52.5 in the Group S and 37.5 in the Group T ( p < 0.001) (Fig. ). Comparison of the difference in scores of each landmark between the two groups There was no significant difference in scores between the two groups in the first four landmarks which include : (1) ME 4-chamber view, (2) ME 2-chamber view, (3) ME long-axis view and (4) ME ascending aortic long axis, while the difference in score was statistically significant in landmarks 5–11 which include : (1) ME ascending aortic short axis; (2) ME aortic valve short axis; (3) ME right ventricle inflow-outflow; (4) ME bicaval; (5) ME descending aortic short axis; (6) ME descending aortic long axis and (7) TG midpapillary short axis. The score of Group S was significantly higher than that of Group T ( p < 0.05) (Table ). Discussion Transesophageal echocardiography (TEE) is a critical cardiac imaging modality essential for anesthesia and perioperative management. However, acquiring and maintaining TEE proficiency demands extensive practice and the accumulation of clinical experience [ ]. Consequently, simulation-based training has emerged as a prominent and effective educational tool in TEE instruction. The present study demonstrates that simulation-based training utilizing a 3D mannequin simulator translates directly into superior live TEE performance within the pediatric population. Specifically, novice residents in the simulation group (Group S) achieved higher image quality and demonstrated greater procedural efficiency compared to those in the traditional apprenticeship group (Group T). By providing residents with the opportunity to practice TEE skills in a controlled, risk-free environment, simulation training helps reduce potential risks associated with real-world patient care [ ]. Previous research has shown that significant advantages in improving learning efficiency, accelerating learning and improving comfort with TEE for cardiovascular medicine fellows compared to traditional training methods [ ]. According to guidelines by Hahn et al. [ ], the views included the mid-esophageal (ME) aortic valve short axis and ME bicaval views require complex, simultaneous manual rotation and tip flexion. Furthermore, transgastric (TG) views require mastering gastric advancement and anteflexion, while imaging the descending aorta necessitates a non-intuitive 180-degree probe rotation. In our study, the advantages of simulation were most pronounced in these technically demanding landmarks (Views 5–11), including the ME ascending aortic short axis, ME aortic valve short axis, and particularly the TG mid-papillary short-axis views. Our results align with previous literature in adult populations, a study found that the simulated training group scored significantly higher on both skill tests and knowledge tests than the non-simulated training group [ ]. Regarding the skills mentioned, the study by Bloch et al. specifically evaluated: (1) Imaging quality scores; (2) Quantification skills (including left ventricular function, fractional area change, and grading of valvular insufficiency); and (3) Clinical interpretation skills (identification of hypovolemia, ventricular failure, and tamponade) [ ]. By demonstrating similar superior outcomes in our study, Group S both in terms of higher clinical scores and shorter examination times further validates the essential role of simulation in improving TEE skills. These findings strongly support the integration of simulation training as a mandatory component of pediatric cardiac anesthesia education. Successful TEE performance requires technical proficiency alongside a sophisticated understanding of pediatric anatomy to ensure safe intubation—a critical concern in small children [ – ]. Our curriculum—comprising only two hours of didactic preparation and one hour of hands-on simulation—demonstrates that foundational TEE competency can be effectively initiated during residency. This model provides a streamlined alternative to prolonged specialized fellowship training for achieving initial clinical proficiency. There are several limitations to this study. First, the fixed size of the residency program necessitated a convenience sample ( n = 44), which may limit the statistical power for secondary outcomes. Second, this study assessed short-term skill acquisition rather than long-term retention or competency. Future TEE education may benefit from combining simulation with clinical practice to reinforce both basic and advanced skills [ , ]. Third, the study was limited to anesthesiology residents; future research should explore personalized and adaptive TEE teaching models [ ]. Lastly, although we observed qualitative improvements in trainee engagement, we did not formally measure confidence or satisfaction using validated scales. Conclusion In summary, this trial provides robust evidence that 3D simulation training significantly improves live TEE performance among novice operators compared to conventional training, contributing valuable insights toward optimizing echocardiography education and enhancing perioperative safety in pediatric cardiac care. Introduction: Why Myocardial Involvement in Systemic Sclerosis Is Underdetected Systemic sclerosis (SSc) is a chronic autoimmune connective tissue disease characterized by immune dysregulation, widespread microvascular dysfunction, and progressive fibrosis affecting multiple organs, including the skin, lungs, gastrointestinal tract, and heart [ , ]. The disease is classified according to the American College of Rheumatology/European League Against Rheumatism (ACR/EULAR) criteria, reflecting its heterogeneous clinical spectrum and multisystem involvement [ ]. Cardiac involvement is one of the most serious complications of SSc and is associated with increased morbidity and mortality, although myocardial involvement often remains underrecognized due to its frequently presentation in early stages [ , ]. Structural myocardial abnormalities are more common than clinically overt disease, highlighting a gap between pathological involvement and clinical detection [ , , ]. A distinctive feature of SSc-related cardiomyopathy is the unique interplay between coronary microvascular dysfunction, diffuse myocardial fibrosis, and arrhythmogenic remodeling. Unlike ischemic cardiomyopathy, myocardial injury in SSc is primarily driven by microvascular abnormalities and immune-mediated processes rather than obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease. This results in diffuse and heterogeneous myocardial involvement, which may predispose to early ventricular dysfunction and increased arrhythmic risk even in the absence of overt structural heart disease. The pathogenesis of myocardial involvement in SSc is multifactorial and involves coronary microvascular dysfunction, immune-mediated inflammation, and progressive myocardial fibrosis [ , ]. These processes lead to recurrent myocardial injury, ventricular dysfunction, and arrhythmogenic remodeling [ , ]. Histopathological studies have demonstrated patchy myocardial fibrosis and small-vessel vasculopathy as characteristic features of cardiac involvement in SSc [ , ]. Importantly, myocardial dysfunction may be present even in asymptomatic patients, suggesting early subclinical disease [ ]. Clinically apparent manifestations, including heart failure and arrhythmias, typically occur later in the disease course [ , ], while cardiovascular complications remain a major contributor to mortality [ , ]. Long-term studies confirm that cardiac and pulmonary vascular involvement are key determinants of survival in SSc [ ]. Several factors contribute to the underdetection of myocardial involvement. Conventional diagnostic methods may lack sensitivity for early disease, and symptoms may be nonspecific or masked by other systemic manifestations [ , ]. In addition, myocardial injury often develops through diffuse and heterogeneous processes that are not easily captured by standard techniques [ ]. These limitations highlight the need for sensitive imaging techniques capable of detecting early and subclinical myocardial involvement. Advances in cardiovascular imaging have substantially improved the detection of subclinical myocardial involvement in SSc. Techniques such as speckle-tracking echocardiography and cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) enable identification of early myocardial dysfunction, microvascular impairment, inflammation, and fibrosis [ , , ]. In particular, CMR techniques, including late gadolinium enhancement (LGE) and parametric mapping, allow for noninvasive assessment of myocardial tissue characteristics [ , ]. Similarly, myocardial strain imaging can detect early ventricular dysfunction even in asymptomatic patients [ , ]. Despite these advances, optimal strategies for screening and monitoring myocardial involvement in SSc remain incompletely defined [ , ]. Given the clinical importance of early detection, there is increasing interest in integrating multimodality cardiovascular imaging into routine clinical evaluation [ , ]. This review therefore aims to provide a focused overview of myocardial involvement in SSc and to highlight the role of contemporary multimodality cardiovascular imaging in its detection, characterization, and clinical management. A narrative literature search was conducted using PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science to identify relevant studies published up to 2025. The search strategy included combinations of predefined keywords using Boolean operators, such as (“systemic sclerosis” OR “scleroderma”) AND (“cardiac involvement” OR “myocardial fibrosis” OR “cardiomyopathy”) AND (“echocardiography” OR “cardiac magnetic resonance” OR “CMR” OR “PET” OR “computed tomography”). Studies were screened based on titles and abstracts, followed by full-text evaluation where appropriate. Priority was given to original studies, systematic reviews, and consensus documents focusing on imaging-based assessment of myocardial involvement in systemic sclerosis. Articles were selected based on their relevance to pathophysiology, diagnostic performance, and clinical applicability of imaging modalities. Non-relevant articles, studies not focused on cardiovascular imaging, and publications lacking sufficient methodological clarity were excluded. Additional relevant studies were identified through manual screening of reference lists. 2. Pathobiology of Systemic Sclerosis Cardiomyopathy Relevant to Imaging Cardiac involvement in SSc results from the interplay of microvascular dysfunction, immune-mediated inflammation, and progressive myocardial fibrosis [ , ]. These processes often develop subclinically and may remain undetected for prolonged periods [ , ]. Understanding these mechanisms is essential because each component can be assessed using specific cardiovascular imaging techniques. Contemporary imaging modalities therefore provide a noninvasive approach to detect and characterize different stages of SSc cardiomyopathy [ , ]. Microvascular Dysfunction and Ischemia Without Epicardial CAD Microvascular dysfunction is a central mechanism in SSc cardiomyopathy and is characterized by structural and functional abnormalities of the coronary microcirculation, leading to impaired myocardial perfusion in the absence of obstructive epicardial coronary artery disease [ , ]. These abnormalities result in reduced coronary flow reserve and recurrent ischemic injury, contributing to progressive myocardial fibrosis [ , ]. Noninvasive imaging techniques such as stress echocardiography, myocardial perfusion imaging, and PET enable assessment of coronary microvascular function and detection of perfusion abnormalities [ , ]. 2.2. Inflammation–Fibrosis Continuum Immune-mediated myocardial inflammation represents a key component of SSc cardiomyopathy and contributes to myocardial injury through activation of profibrotic pathways [ , ]. This inflammation–fibrosis continuum leads to diffuse or patchy myocardial remodeling, which may impair contractility and promote ventricular dysfunction [ , ]. Cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR), particularly with parametric mapping techniques including T1 and T2 mapping and extracellular volume quantification, enables noninvasive assessment of myocardial inflammation and diffuse fibrosis [ , ]. 2.3. Conduction System Disease and Arrhythmogenic Substrate Myocardial fibrosis and microvascular injury contribute to the development of arrhythmogenic substrates in SSc. Structural remodeling disrupts normal electrical conduction pathways and promotes electrical heterogeneity, increasing susceptibility to arrhythmias [ , ]. Imaging techniques, particularly CMR with late gadolinium enhancement and echocardiographic strain imaging, enable identification of structural abnormalities associated with increased arrhythmic risk [ , ]. These pathophysiological mechanisms provide the foundation for the use of advanced cardiovascular imaging techniques aimed at detecting microvascular dysfunction, inflammation, and myocardial fibrosis in SSc. 3. Clinical Phenotypes and Outcomes to Be Targeted by Imaging Cardiac involvement in SSc encompasses a broad spectrum of clinical phenotypes ranging from subclinical myocardial abnormalities to overt heart failure, arrhythmias, and pulmonary hypertension. Because myocardial disease in SSc often evolves gradually and may remain asymptomatic in its early stages, imaging plays a critical role in identifying clinically relevant cardiac phenotypes before irreversible myocardial damage occurs [ , ]. Contemporary cardiovascular imaging therefore aims not only to detect structural myocardial abnormalities but also to identify patients at increased risk of adverse clinical outcomes. Observational cohort studies have shown that cardiac involvement is frequently underestimated in routine clinical evaluation and may only become clinically apparent in advanced stages of the disease [ , ]. One of the most important clinical phenotypes targeted by imaging is subclinical myocardial dysfunction. Numerous studies have demonstrated that patients with SSc may develop early ventricular dysfunction even in the absence of overt cardiac symptoms. Subclinical abnormalities in myocardial mechanics, particularly reduced global longitudinal strain (GLS), may precede detectable reductions in left ventricular ejection fraction and can be identified using speckle-tracking echocardiography [ , ]. These findings are supported by broader echocardiographic research demonstrating that myocardial deformation imaging provides sensitive markers of early myocardial dysfunction before conventional parameters become abnormal [ , ]. Similarly, cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) studies have shown that diffuse myocardial fibrosis and inflammation may be present even in patients without clinically apparent cardiac disease [ ]. Early myocardial abnormalities have also been demonstrated in treatment-naïve patients with connective tissue diseases using CMR, further supporting the concept of subclinical cardiomyopathy [ ]. Identification of this early phenotype is important because it may represent a potentially reversible stage of myocardial injury. Another clinically important phenotype is overt ventricular dysfunction and heart failure. As outlined in , progressive myocardial fibrosis and microvascular injury represent the key underlying mechanisms contributing to this phenotype. Both left and right ventricular dysfunction have been described in SSc and are associated with adverse clinical outcomes [ , ]. Imaging modalities such as echocardiography and CMR are essential for assessing ventricular function, myocardial structure, and ventricular remodeling, allowing clinicians to differentiate primary myocardial involvement from secondary cardiac complications such as pulmonary hypertension-related right ventricular dysfunction [ , ]. Clinical guidelines emphasize the importance of comprehensive cardiac evaluation in patients with heart failure, including assessment of ventricular function, structural abnormalities, and myocardial tissue characteristics [ , ]. Early recognition of ventricular dysfunction is particularly important because it may influence therapeutic strategies and clinical monitoring. Pulmonary hypertension-related cardiac involvement represents another major clinical phenotype in SSc. Pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) is a well-recognized complication of the disease and contributes significantly to morbidity and mortality [ , ]. Screening strategies have been developed to facilitate early detection of PAH in SSc because of its major impact on survival [ , ]. Imaging plays a central role in screening and risk stratification of patients with suspected PAH, particularly through echocardiographic assessment of right ventricular size, function, and pulmonary pressures [ ]. Because right ventricular dysfunction is a major determinant of prognosis in PAH, imaging evaluation of right heart structure and function is essential in the management of these patients. Echocardiographic assessment of right ventricular function and pulmonary hemodynamics has therefore become a key component of screening algorithms for SSc-associated pulmonary vascular disease [ ]. Arrhythmias and conduction abnormalities constitute another clinically significant phenotype of SSc cardiac involvement. As previously discussed, myocardial fibrosis and microvascular injury create arrhythmogenic substrates that predispose patients to atrial and ventricular arrhythmias. Fibrotic remodeling of the myocardium can disrupt normal electrical conduction pathways and create heterogeneous conduction properties that increase the risk of ventricular arrhythmias and sudden cardiac death [ ]. Imaging modalities such as CMR can detect myocardial fibrosis through LGE, which has been associated with increased arrhythmic risk and adverse cardiovascular outcomes [ , ]. Identifying patients with structural substrates for arrhythmias may therefore facilitate targeted rhythm monitoring and early therapeutic intervention. Importantly, cardiovascular imaging also plays a key role in predicting long-term clinical outcomes in patients with SSc. Several studies have demonstrated that imaging biomarkers, including impaired myocardial strain, ventricular dysfunction, and myocardial fibrosis, are associated with increased risk of cardiovascular events and mortality [ , ]. Long-term observational studies have also shown that cardiovascular complications remain a major determinant of mortality in SSc [ ]. These findings highlight the prognostic value of imaging-based risk stratification in SSc and support the integration of multimodality imaging into routine clinical assessment. Given the heterogeneity of cardiac manifestations in SSc, a comprehensive imaging strategy is often required to identify the full spectrum of clinically relevant phenotypes. Multimodality imaging approaches integrating echocardiography, CMR, CT, and nuclear imaging may provide complementary information regarding myocardial structure, function, perfusion, inflammation, and coronary anatomy [ , ], as summarized in . Advances in cardiovascular imaging have also improved the detection of myocardial abnormalities in rheumatologic diseases, particularly through the use of quantitative CMR techniques and advanced echocardiographic deformation imaging [ , ]. Such integrated assessment is increasingly recognized as an essential component of contemporary evaluation of myocardial involvement in SSc and may improve early detection, prognostic stratification, and clinical management of affected patients. 4. Conventional and advanced echocardiographic techniques allow for evaluation of ventricular size, systolic and diastolic function, pulmonary pressures, and myocardial mechanics, making echocardiography a key tool for both screening and longitudinal monitoring of cardiac disease in SSc [ , ]. Early echocardiographic studies demonstrated that cardiac abnormalities in SSc may be detected even in patients without overt cardiovascular symptoms, highlighting the value of routine echocardiographic surveillance [ ]. Cardiac abnormalities detected by echocardiography in SSc may include ventricular dysfunction, diastolic abnormalities, right ventricular remodeling, and indirect signs of pulmonary hypertension. Importantly, echocardiography can identify early functional changes before the development of overt clinical manifestations, enabling earlier detection of myocardial involvement [ ]. Contemporary echocardiographic approaches increasingly incorporate advanced techniques such as speckle-tracking strain imaging and stress echocardiography, which provide additional insights into myocardial mechanics and coronary microvascular function. The growing use of quantitative echocardiographic techniques has further improved the ability to detect subtle myocardial dysfunction in patients with SSc [ , ]. 4.1. 4.1. Standard Transthoracic Echocardiography—LV/RV Size and Function, Diastology Standard transthoracic echocardiography (TTE) is the cornerstone of cardiac evaluation in patients with SSc. It allows for assessment of left and right ventricular size, systolic function, wall motion abnormalities, and valvular structure, as well as estimation of pulmonary pressures. These parameters are essential for identifying both primary myocardial involvement and secondary cardiac complications associated with SSc [ ]. Guidelines from professional societies emphasize the importance of standardized echocardiographic measurements when evaluating ventricular structure and function. Parameters such as left ventricular ejection fraction, chamber dimensions, and right ventricular function indices are recommended for routine clinical assessment [ , ]. In addition, recommendations for image acquisition and quantitative evaluation of cardiac mechanics have been developed to improve reproducibility and standardization of echocardiographic measurements [ , ]. In SSc patients, conventional echocardiography may demonstrate subtle ventricular abnormalities, including mild systolic dysfunction, chamber dilation, or regional wall motion abnormalities associated with myocardial fibrosis or microvascular ischemia. Several cohort studies have demonstrated that echocardiographic abnormalities are common in SSc patients even in the absence of overt cardiac symptoms [ ]. Right ventricular assessment is particularly important in SSc because right ventricular dysfunction may reflect either primary myocardial involvement or secondary effects of pulmonary hypertension. Echocardiographic parameters such as tricuspid annular plane systolic excursion (TAPSE), right ventricular fractional area change, and right ventricular dimensions are commonly used to evaluate right ventricular function in this population [ ]. Advanced echocardiographic techniques such as three-dimensional echocardiography may further improve quantification of right ventricular volumes and function [ ]. Although conventional echocardiographic parameters may remain normal in early disease stages, they provide an important baseline for monitoring disease progression and evaluating therapeutic response in patients with established cardiac involvement. 4.2. Tissue Doppler Imaging and Diastolic Dysfunction in Systemic Sclerosis Diastolic dysfunction is one of the most frequently reported echocardiographic abnormalities in patients with SSc and may occur even in the absence of overt systolic dysfunction. Tissue Doppler imaging (TDI) provides a sensitive method for evaluating myocardial relaxation and ventricular filling pressures by measuring myocardial velocities at the mitral annulus [ ]. Early studies have demonstrated that patients with SSc often exhibit impaired myocardial relaxation and increased left ventricular filling pressures, reflecting early myocardial involvement related to diffuse fibrosis and microvascular ischemia [ , ]. Tissue Doppler parameters such as reduced early diastolic velocity (e′) and increased E/e′ ratio have been associated with subclinical myocardial dysfunction in this population. Assessment of diastolic function is particularly important because diastolic abnormalities may represent one of the earliest manifestations of SSc cardiomyopathy. Current echocardiographic guidelines recommend a comprehensive evaluation of diastolic function incorporating multiple parameters, including transmitral inflow patterns, tissue Doppler velocities, and left atrial size [ ]. Diastolic abnormalities may reflect underlying diffuse myocardial fibrosis and microvascular disease, which are hallmarks of SSc cardiomyopathy [ , ]. 4.3. Speckle-Tracking Strain Imaging (LV GLS, RV Strain, LA Strain) Speckle-tracking echocardiography (STE) has emerged as a powerful tool for detecting subtle myocardial dysfunction in SSc. This technique allows for quantitative assessment of myocardial deformation by measuring strain parameters, including GLS, which reflects longitudinal myocardial fiber shortening [ , ]. Standardization of strain imaging methodology has been emphasized by international task force documents to improve inter-vendor reproducibility and clinical applicability [ , , , , , , , ]. Several studies have demonstrated that patients with SSc may exhibit reduced GLS despite preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, suggesting the presence of subclinical myocardial dysfunction [ , ]. Reduced GLS has been associated with myocardial fibrosis detected by cardiac magnetic resonance imaging and may serve as an early marker of SSc cardiomyopathy. Speckle-tracking techniques can also evaluate right ventricular and left atrial strain, providing additional information about cardiac involvement. Right ventricular longitudinal strain has been shown to detect early right ventricular dysfunction and may be particularly useful in patients with SSc-related pulmonary hypertension [ ]. Other imaging studies have confirmed that focal myocardial fibrosis detected by CMR may correspond to areas of microvascular ischemic injury and fibrotic remodeling [ ]. Similar observations are emerging in connective tissue diseases, where distinct cardiovascular phenotypes identified by CMR have been shown to be associated with clinical outcomes in systemic sclerosis [ ]. Perfusion SPECT/PET and Microvascular Ischemia Myocardial perfusion imaging using SPECT or PET provides important information regarding coronary circulation and myocardial blood flow. Consequently, perfusion imaging techniques may help identify microvascular ischemia that may not be detectable using conventional coronary angiography. Quantitative PET assessment of myocardial blood flow has therefore emerged as an important tool for evaluating coronary microvascular dysfunction and predicting cardiovascular risk [ ]. Because cardiac manifestations of SSc arise from a complex interplay of microvascular dysfunction, inflammation, and myocardial fibrosis, a multimodality imaging strategy is generally recommended to comprehensively evaluate myocardial structure, function, and tissue characteristics [ , ]. Such an approach enables clinicians to identify different components of SSc cardiomyopathy and tailor diagnostic and monitoring strategies according to individual patient risk profiles. A stepwise approach to imaging is recommended, starting with echocardiography and progressing to advanced modalities based on clinical and imaging findings. 11.1. Baseline Screening At the time of diagnosis, patients with SSc should undergo a comprehensive cardiovascular evaluation, including clinical assessment, electrocardiography, and TTE. Echocardiography represents the first-line imaging modality for cardiac screening because it allows for noninvasive assessment of ventricular size and function, diastolic parameters, pulmonary pressures, and right ventricular performance [ , ]. Standard echocardiographic measurements provide important baseline information regarding cardiac structure and function and facilitate longitudinal monitoring of disease progression. Advanced echocardiographic techniques, particularly speckle-tracking strain imaging, may further improve the detection of early myocardial dysfunction. Reduced GLS has been shown to identify subclinical myocardial involvement in patients with SSc even when left ventricular ejection fraction remains preserved [ , ]. Because early myocardial abnormalities may precede clinically apparent cardiac disease, incorporation of myocardial strain analysis into routine echocardiographic assessment may enhance screening strategies in SSc clinics. In addition to cardiac evaluation, echocardiography also plays a key role in screening for pulmonary hypertension, a major complication of SSc. Assessment of TRV, right ventricular size, and right ventricular systolic function allows for identification of patients who may require further evaluation for PAH using right heart catheterization [ , ]. If abnormalities are detected or clinical suspicion persists, further evaluation with advanced imaging modalities, particularly CMR, is recommended. 11.2. Advanced Imaging Assessment When echocardiographic abnormalities are detected or when clinical suspicion of myocardial involvement persists despite normal findings, CMR should be performed as the next-line imaging modality [ , ]. CMR is particularly indicated for the detection of myocardial fibrosis and inflammation using LGE and parametric mapping techniques [ , ]. In patients with symptoms suggestive of ischemia or in those with cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac CT may be considered to exclude obstructive coronary artery disease [ ]. Nuclear imaging techniques such as PET or SPECT may be used in selected cases to assess coronary microvascular dysfunction or myocardial inflammation, particularly when other imaging findings are inconclusive [ , ]. In clinical practice, abnormal global longitudinal strain or regional strain abnormalities on echocardiography should prompt further evaluation with CMR, even in the presence of preserved ejection fraction. Nuclear imaging techniques, including PET, should be considered in selected patients with suspected coronary microvascular dysfunction or when findings from echocardiography and CMR are inconclusive. In clinical practice, a stepwise decision-oriented approach may be applied. If global longitudinal strain is reduced or regional strain abnormalities are present despite preserved left ventricular ejection fraction, further evaluation with CMR should be considered to assess myocardial fibrosis and inflammation. If CMR findings are inconclusive or if there is a high suspicion of microvascular dysfunction, PET imaging may be performed to quantify coronary flow reserve. In patients with symptoms suggestive of ischemia or relevant cardiovascular risk factors, cardiac CT should be considered to exclude obstructive coronary artery disease. Conversely, if initial echocardiographic findings are normal and clinical suspicion is low, routine follow-up with periodic echocardiography may be sufficient. 11.3. Conclusions Myocardial involvement represents an important yet frequently underrecognized manifestation of SSc. The complex interplay of coronary microvascular dysfunction, immune-mediated inflammation, and progressive myocardial fibrosis contributes to the development of SSc cardiomyopathy and may ultimately lead to ventricular dysfunction, arrhythmias, heart failure, and increased risk of sudden cardiac death [ , ]. Importantly, myocardial abnormalities may develop long before clinical symptoms become apparent, underscoring the need for sensitive diagnostic approaches capable of identifying subclinical disease. Advances in cardiovascular imaging have substantially improved the detection and characterization of myocardial involvement in SSc [ ]. Echocardiography remains the cornerstone of initial cardiac evaluation and longitudinal monitoring, enabling assessment of ventricular function, myocardial mechanics, and pulmonary pressures [ , ]. Techniques such as speckle-tracking strain imaging have further enhanced the ability to detect subtle impairments in myocardial function that may precede overt systolic dysfunction [ ]. CMR has emerged as the reference imaging modality for comprehensive myocardial tissue characterization. Techniques including LGE and parametric mapping allow for noninvasive detection of myocardial fibrosis and inflammation, providing valuable insights into the underlying pathophysiological processes of SSc cardiomyopathy [ , ]. In addition, nuclear imaging techniques such as PET and SPECT can assess coronary microvascular dysfunction, inflammatory activity, and emerging molecular targets related to fibrotic remodeling [ , ]. Cardiac CT may serve as a complementary modality for excluding obstructive CAD and evaluating thoracic structural abnormalities [ ]. The integration of these imaging modalities into structured multimodality algorithms enables more accurate detection of subclinical myocardial disease, facilitates monitoring of disease progression and therapeutic response, and improves risk stratification for adverse cardiovascular outcomes [ , ]. Imaging biomarkers such as myocardial strain abnormalities, diffuse myocardial fibrosis detected by CMR, and impaired CFR have demonstrated potential prognostic value and may help identify patients at increased risk of cardiac complications [ , ]. Future developments in cardiovascular imaging, including AI–assisted analysis, radiomics, and novel molecular imaging tracers, may further enhance the ability to detect early myocardial involvement and quantify disease activity. These advances may also facilitate the use of imaging biomarkers as surrogate endpoints in clinical trials evaluating emerging therapies for SSc [ , ]. In conclusion, myocardial involvement in SSc represents a multifaceted and clinically significant complication that requires a comprehensive diagnostic approach. Multimodality cardiovascular imaging plays a central role in the detection, characterization, and monitoring of cardiac disease in SSc and is increasingly recognized as an essential component of contemporary patient management. Continued research integrating advanced imaging techniques with clinical and molecular data will be crucial for improving early diagnosis, refining risk stratification, and ultimately enhancing outcomes for patients with SSc.
